title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

content.overview: BSA s. 4, Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction, is an evidentiary provision in the Relevancy of facts cluster. Analyse it through the separate questions of relevancy, admissibility, proof, burden and probative weight, and check BSA s. 170 for proceedings governed by the repeal and savings rule. Historical concordance: Indian Evidence Act s. 6.

content.study:
Current-law identity
BSA s. 4 governs relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction within Chapter II - Relevancy of facts. The provision must be read with its enacted clauses, explanations, illustrations and connected provisions BSA s. 3, BSA s. 5. Historical concordance: Indian Evidence Act s. 6.

The forensic distinction
Relevancy asks whether a fact has the statutory connection required by the Adhiniyam. Admissibility asks whether the Court may receive that relevant material under the rules of exclusion, privilege, form and foundation. Proof asks whether the admitted material establishes the fact to the required standard. Probative weight asks how much reliance the Court should place on it. A relevant fact is not automatically admissible, and admissibility is not proof of the ultimate fact.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the fact in issue, the fact sought to be introduced and the party tendering it.
2. State the exact rule in BSA s. 4, including every condition, explanation, proviso and illustration.
3. Classify the material as oral, documentary, electronic, real or circumstantial evidence.
4. Test directness, hearsay, privilege, primary or secondary evidence, authentication and statutory certificate requirements.
5. Identify the party bearing the initial burden under BSA s. 104 and any special-knowledge rule under s. 109.
6. Separate admissibility from the weight ultimately assigned after cross-examination and the complete record.

Electronic records and constitutional limits
Electronic and digital records are documents under BSA. Where a computer output, email, messaging record, CCTV export, call record, server log or device image is tendered through the statutory route, check BSA s. 63 and its certificate requirements. The certificate is not a substitute for relevance, authenticity, chain of custody or proof of the fact asserted. Evidence must also respect Articles 20(3), 21 and 14 of the Constitution, privilege rules and fair-trial disclosure.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, identify the fact in issue, show the statutory relevancy link, answer the admissibility objection, establish the foundation, identify the burden and standard, and explain the probative consequence. Do not cite the historical Evidence Act number as the current rule after 1 July 2024 except as concordance. Do not convert a missing certificate, hearsay statement or weak foundation into an automatic finding on the merits without analysing the applicable statutory consequence.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Evidentiary Foundation
sections.body:
BSA s. 4 regulates relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction within Relevancy of facts.
The statutory scheme seeks reliable adjudication by limiting proof to legally relevant and properly received material.
Read the provision with the constitutional values of fair trial, privilege, reliability and equality of arms.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Exceptions and Connected Rules
sections.body:
Deconstruct every clause of BSA s. 4; do not replace the enacted rule with a one-line Evidence Act summary.
Read it with BSA s. 3, BSA s. 5. Connected provisions may control foundation, exclusion, presumptions, witnesses or the mode of proof.
Historical concordance assists comparison only and is not the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Relevancy, Admissibility and Proof Ingredients
sections.body:
First ingredient: identify the fact in issue or the statutory relevancy link.
Second ingredient: satisfy any exclusion, privilege, directness, primary-document or foundation rule.
Third ingredient: prove authenticity and the source or maker where the form of evidence requires it.
Fourth ingredient: apply the correct burden and standard, then distinguish admissibility from probative weight.

sections.heading: BSA Burdens, Presumptions and Electronic Records
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; the party asserting the legal proposition must establish its foundation.
BSA s. 109 addresses facts especially within knowledge. It does not erase the initial burden or permit conviction on an unproved charge.
For electronic records, examine BSA s. 63 certificate, device or system identity, production method, integrity, custody and the distinction between admissibility and weight.

sections.heading: Trial Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Repeal Savings
sections.body:
Apply BSA s. 4 at the correct stage of trial or inquiry and identify whether the objection concerns tender, marking, admissibility, proof or final weight.
For proceedings governed by the post-1 July 2024 evidence regime, cite BSA. For proceedings saved by s. 170, identify the applicable Indian Evidence Act route before arguing the consequence.
Check the governing procedural statute and any special limitation rule for the application or appeal; evidence law itself does not create a universal limitation period.

examples.title: Example 1 - Foundation and admissibility satisfied
examples.body: A party identifies the fact in issue, establishes the statutory relevancy link under s. 4, proves the source and authenticity of the record, and satisfies the applicable documentary or electronic foundation. The Court may receive the material and then assess its weight.

examples.title: Example 2 - Relevancy does not cure a defect
examples.body: A party offers a relevant screenshot or hearsay statement but cannot satisfy the applicable statutory foundation, certificate, directness or privilege rule. The Court must analyse admissibility separately instead of treating logical relevance as automatic proof.

hypotheticals.question: Whether the material is relevant and admissible under BSA s. 4, and what proof and burden consequences follow.
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the fact in issue and the statutory relevancy route. 2. Test the form of evidence: direct oral evidence, documentary evidence, electronic record, hearsay or privileged communication. 3. Check the applicable foundation and BSA s. 63 certificate where digital material is tendered. 4. Place the initial burden under s. 104 and use s. 109 only after the foundation for special knowledge is established. 5. Separate admissibility from credibility and final probative weight.

misconceptions.trap: Citing only the old Evidence Act number for s. 4.
misconceptions.correction: Use BSA s. 4 for the current regime and mention the historical number only as concordance or when applying the s. 170 savings rule.

misconceptions.trap: Relevancy automatically means admissibility and proof.
misconceptions.correction: Relevancy, admissibility, proof and probative weight are separate forensic inquiries.

misconceptions.trap: BSA s. 109 reverses the entire burden of proof.
misconceptions.correction: The initial burden remains with the party asserting the legal proposition; special knowledge operates only on the facts within that statutory rule.

cases.name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
cases.facts: The case concerned the proof and certification of electronic records tendered in election litigation.
cases.issue: Whether the statutory certificate requirement for computer outputs is mandatory and when secondary electronic evidence may be received.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The certificate requirement is a condition precedent for admissibility of the relevant electronic record output, subject to the statutory route and the Court's power to facilitate production where the facts justify it.
cases.holding: The Constitution Bench clarified the certificate rule and overruled the contrary view to the extent necessary.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 4 concerns electronic records or digital proof; it does not decide the relevancy or admissibility of every non-digital item.

cases.name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
cases.facts: The Court examined the mode of proving electronic records in an election dispute.
cases.issue: Whether electronic records could be admitted without compliance with the statutory certificate route.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Electronic evidence must be proved through the special statutory requirements applicable to computer outputs; ordinary secondary-evidence principles cannot bypass that route.
cases.holding: The earlier contrary approach was displaced and the certificate discipline was reaffirmed.
cases.relevance: Use only for digital evidence issues connected with s. 4; distinguish it from ordinary oral, physical-document or privilege questions.

cases.name: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra
cases.facts: The Court assessed a prosecution based substantially on circumstantial evidence.
cases.issue: What standard must circumstantial evidence meet before it can support a criminal conviction.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive in tendency, and form a complete chain excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
cases.holding: The Court restated the safeguards for conviction on circumstantial evidence.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 4 concerns circumstantial proof or inference; do not use it as a substitute for a section-specific relevancy rule.

BSA s. 4 governs relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction. Read it with BSA s. 3, BSA s. 5, then identify the relevancy, admissibility, proof and burden rules.

Comprehensive doctrinal analysis of Res Gestae (facts forming part of the same transaction) under Section 4 BSA, modernizing the rule to include electronic communications and contemporaneous digital feeds.
Statutory text strictly follows Act No. 47 of 2023, s. 4.

learningObjectives: Master the doctrine of Res Gestae under Section 4 BSA (replacing Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872).
Understand the foundational test: facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction.
Analyze the temporal and physical scope: whether the connected facts occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.
Evaluate the modern electronic application: live audio-video calls, digital transmissions, and contemporaneous CCTV feeds as res gestae.
Distinguish admissible res gestae statements from inadmissible post-incident narrative hearsay.
enhancement.definition: BSA s. 4 codifies the doctrine of Res Gestae (facts forming part of the same transaction). It provides: Facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction, are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Spontaneity, contemporaneity, and the exception to the rule against hearsay. Statements or acts so intimately interwoven with the principal event that they are spontaneous and contemporaneous—excluding any possibility of fabrication or concoction—are admitted as part of the transaction itself.
statutoryFramework: Chapter II — Relevancy of Facts, BSA s. 4.
Core Doctrinal Gateway: Relevancy of collateral facts that form part of the same transaction as the fact in issue.
Spatiotemporal Flexibility: Explicitly relevant whether occurring at the same time and place or at different times and places.
Exceptions to Hearsay: Serves as one of the primary statutory exceptions to the exclusionary rule against hearsay evidence.
Electronic Integration: Operates alongside Section 63 BSA for contemporaneous audio-video feeds, voice notes, and live streaming.
essentialIngredients: The existence of a fact in issue (the principal disputed act or crime).
The existence of collateral facts, acts, or spontaneous declarations sought to be proved.
A continuous nexus of proximity of time, unity of place, continuity of action, and community of purpose linking the collateral facts to the principal event.
Contemporaneity and spontaneity: the declaration or act must be substantially contemporaneous with the transaction, without interval allowing deliberation or concoction.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 4 BSA codifies the venerable common law doctrine of *res gestae*, replacing Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. It forms a crucial statutory exception to the fundamental rule that hearsay evidence is inadmissible.

The rationale behind Section 4 is that certain acts or utterances are so closely connected with the principal crime that they form part of the event itself. Spontaneous exclamations uttered during the commission of a crime carry high probative reliability because the human mind, operating under sudden pressure, has no opportunity to fabricate or reflect.

To satisfy the test of "forming part of the same transaction", courts apply three rigorous criteria:
1. **Contemporaneity:** The statement or act must be contemporaneous with the event, or made immediately after it so that the speaker’s mind was still dominated by the occurrence (*Gentela Vijayavardhan Rao* test). If there is an interval allowing the declarant to reflect, fabricate, or narrate a past history, the statement ceases to be res gestae and degenerates into inadmissible hearsay.
2. **Continuity of Action and Purpose:** The acts, even if occurring at different times and places, must be connected by an unbroken chain of cause and effect.
3. **Modern Electronic Expansion:** In modern digital trials, Section 4 applies to real-time electronic phenomena: a victim’s frantic live phone call or voice message recorded on a bystander’s phone while fleeing an attacker, or unbroken CCTV footage tracking a getaway vehicle across different intersections.
examples: Teaching illustration (Admissible Res Gestae — Frantic Cry): Accused A enters a house and shoots victim V. Immediately upon hearing the gunshot, neighbour N rushes out and sees A running away with a pistol, while dying V screams: "A has shot me!" The cry of V and the sighting by N form part of the same transaction under Section 4 BSA; N’s testimony regarding V’s statement is admissible as res gestae, not excluded as hearsay.

Teaching illustration (Inadmissible Narrative Hearsay): B is assaulted in an alley at 8:00 PM. The attacker flees. At 10:30 PM (two and a half hours later), B reaches home, rests, and then recounts the story to his brother. The brother’s testimony regarding what B told him is not admissible under Section 4: the temporal gap allowed for reflection, destroying spontaneity.
distinctions: BSA s. 4 (Res Gestae) vs BSA s. 26 (Dying Declaration): Section 4 requires contemporaneous statements forming part of the same transaction (whether the declarant lives or dies); Section 26 applies to statements made by a deceased person regarding the cause of death, irrespective of whether made immediately during the transaction or hours/days later.

BSA s. 4 vs BSA s. 6 (Conduct): Section 4 covers facts and spontaneous utterances forming the core transaction; Section 6 covers preceding motive/preparation or subsequent conduct influenced by the fact in issue.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a frantic voice note sent by a kidnapping victim via WhatsApp to her friend at the exact moment she was being forced into a vehicle is admissible under Section 4 BSA.
Rule: Under Section 4 BSA, spontaneous declarations made contemporaneously with the commission of an offence form part of the same transaction and are admissible as res gestae.
Application: The voice note was generated in real time during the abduction, capturing the ambient struggle and screams; there was zero interval for fabrication or afterthought.
Conclusion: The audio recording forms part of the same transaction and is admissible as substantive res gestae evidence under Section 4 BSA (subject to Section 63 electronic certification).

shortAnswer: Define Res Gestae under Section 4 BSA.
State the core test: facts so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction.
Highlight contemporaneity as the safeguard against hearsay.

keyTakeaways: BSA s. 4 codifies the doctrine of Res Gestae (facts forming part of the same transaction).
Acts and utterances connected with the crime are relevant even if occurring at different times and places.
Spontaneity and contemporaneity are mandatory to exclude concoction or fabrication.
Applies to live digital recordings, phone calls, and emergency transmissions in modern litigation.
